role: Editor of the spoken lines. No fact was changed: where a hook or a closing moved, the new one is drawn from the same fragment or its reviewed Codex records, as source says.
method: Every line was read aloud for the five beats in order, a term a guest would need explained, a list longer than three, and a sale that ends on the pour.

Openings were tallied by the first one, two and three words after the grape name; closings by their first two words and by DNA and name phrases; sales by hook and by the first words of the pour; four and five word phrases shared across grapes were listed and the recited ones broken up.
Edits were exact substring replacements on the fragment text, field by field, so the files keep their layout; every fragment linted sound after each round.

lines.s45.was: Albariño grows within sight of the Atlantic, in Rías Baixas, on the rainy green coast of north west Spain. It tastes of white peach, apricot and lime, with a salty edge like sea spray. It is dry and light, with high, mouth watering acidity. Most is made in steel tanks and bottled young, with no oak. Across the river Miño, in Portugal, it is called Alvarinho and is often a touch riper and rounder. It is a wine for shellfish: oysters, grilled prawns or octopus. The vines are trained overhead on granite posts, high enough to walk beneath, so the sea wind can dry the grapes after rain.

lines.s45.was: Gewürztraminer announces itself before the glass reaches you. It is a pink skinned grape, and its home is Alsace, in the east of France. It smells of lychee, rose petal and ginger, and it is full and soft, low in acidity and often just off dry. The cellar keeps out of the way: no new oak, only ripe fruit. Alsace tends to be rich and heady, while California's cool coast is usually lighter and fresher. Pour it with washed rind cheese, foie gras or a fragrant Thai curry. Gewürz is the German word for spice, and Traminer is named for Tramin, a village in the Italian Alps.

lines.s45.was: Grüner Veltliner is the peppery one. It is Austria's own white grape, grown along the Danube west of Vienna and across the rolling country to the north. lines.s45.was: Riesling is the white that hides nothing: no oak and no cream, only the fruit and the place. Its home is Germany, on the steep slate banks of the Mosel and along the Rhine. It tastes of lime, green apple and white peach, and with years in bottle it gains a note like petrol. It is light, with piercing acidity, and it runs from bone dry to honey sweet. Germany often leaves a touch of sweetness at low alcohol, while Australia ferments it fully dry. Pour it with crab, smoked trout or anything with chilli. The first record of it is a bill for vines dated 1435.

lines.s45.was: Sauvignon Blanc is at home in the upper Loire, in Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, and it found a second home in Marlborough, New Zealand. It smells of grapefruit, gooseberry and fresh cut grass, and it is dry, light and sharply refreshing. Most of it is fermented cold in steel, with no oak, to keep that freshness. The Loire tends to be quieter and flinty, while Marlborough is louder, with passion fruit on top. Pour it with goat's cheese, oysters or anything with green herbs. Its name comes from the French word for wild, and it is one of the two parents of Cabernet Sauvignon.

lines.s45.was: Torrontés plays one trick: it smells sweet and drinks dry. It is Argentina's own white grape, at home around Cafayate in the far north west, where vines stand over a mile high in desert sun. The scent is rose petal, jasmine and ripe peach. The taste is dry, light and fresh, with a faint bitter twist. Oak would smother that perfume, so the wine is made in cool steel tanks and bottled young. Pour it with empanadas, ceviche or anything with a little chilli heat. It arose by chance in Argentina, a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and the mission grape the Spanish brought.

lines.s45.was: Cabernet Franc is the Cabernet that came first, and its home today is the Loire Valley, in Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny. It tastes of raspberry and redcurrant, with violet and a streak of pencil shavings and green bell pepper. It is medium in body, bright and fresh, with fine tannin. The Loire raises it with little new oak, while Argentina and California often make it darker, riper and rounder. Serve it a little cool, with roast chicken, charcuterie or goat's cheese. Crossed by chance with Sauvignon Blanc, it gave the world Cabernet Sauvignon, and it is a parent of Merlot too.

lines.s45.was: Grenache needs heat, and finds it all round the Mediterranean, above all in the southern Rhône and Spain. It tastes of ripe strawberry, raspberry and kirsch, with a little white pepper. The colour is pale, the tannin soft and the alcohol high. It is often raised in concrete or old casks and blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre. The Rhône and Spain tend to be savoury, with dried thyme and rosemary, while Australia is often brighter and fruitier. Pour it with roast lamb, grilled sausages or a slow braise. It most likely began in Aragon, in northern Spain, as Garnacha, and went with that kingdom to Sardinia and southern France.

lines.s45.was: Merlot is the soft heart of red Bordeaux, and on the Right Bank, in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, it leads the blend. It tastes of ripe plum and black cherry, with a note of chocolate, and it feels round and smooth, with gentle tannin. A year or more in oak barrels adds cedar and vanilla. Bordeaux tends to be firmer and more savoury, while California is typically plusher and riper. Pour it with roast duck, mushrooms or a slow braise. Its name is thought to come from merle, the French for blackbird, a bird as dark as the grape and said to be fond of it.

lines.s45.was: Nebbiolo looks gentle and is not. It is the grape of Barolo and Barbaresco, from the Langhe hills around Alba in Piedmont. The glass is pale garnet, with sour cherry, rose petal and tar, but the tannin grips hard and the acidity is high. The law holds Barolo back for more than three years, and many cellars still age it in large old casks that add little taste of wood. Pour it with braised beef, a mushroom risotto or anything under white truffle. Its name is thought to come from nebbia, the fog that fills the valleys when it is picked in October.

lines.s45.was: Sangiovese makes Chianti, Brunello and Vino Nobile, though the labels rarely say so. It is the red of Tuscany, grown on the hills from Florence south to Montalcino. In the glass it is sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried oregano, usually medium in body, with high acidity and a dusty, drying tannin. Brunello is Sangiovese alone, aged at least two years in oak, while Chianti Classico must be at least four fifths Sangiovese. It wants food: pasta in a meat ragù, a grilled steak or aged pecorino. DNA work suggests its parents are Ciliegiolo, still grown in Tuscany, and an almost lost vine found near Naples.

lines.s45.was: Syrah and Shiraz are one grape under two names. Its home is the northern Rhône, on the steep river slopes of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie. It is deep purple and tastes of blackberry, blueberry and cracked black pepper, often with a savoury note of black olive or smoked meat. It is medium to full bodied, with firm tannin, and usually aged in oak. The Rhône tends to be peppery and savoury, while Australian Shiraz is typically riper and richer, with chocolate and vanilla. Pour it with grilled lamb, venison or a peppered steak. Australia has grown it since 1832, and the Barossa still picks from vines planted in the 1840s.

lines.s45.was: Tempranillo is Spain's own red, the grape of Rioja on the upper Ebro and, as Tinto Fino, of Ribera del Duero on the high plateau. It tastes of strawberry, red plum and dried cherry, with leather and tobacco, at medium weight with a fresh, fine grip. The cellar does the rest. Traditional Rioja spends years in American oak barrels, which add vanilla, coconut and dill, and the label says how long: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva. Ribera is darker and firmer, more often in French oak. Pour it with roast lamb, chorizo or Manchego. Temprano means early, and the grape earns the name, ripening weeks before most of Spain's other reds.

lines.s45.was: Assyrtiko is a white grape grown on what is left of a volcano: the hot, dry Greek island of Santorini. The vines stand in ash and pumice, each coiled into a basket on the ground against the wind. The wine tastes of lemon, underripe peach and sea salt, with a stony edge. It is bone dry, and its acidity stays piercing even in that heat. Most is made in steel, and a riper, oaked style is called Nykteri. Assyrtiko is made for oysters, grilled octopus or a whole fish with lemon. The vines grow on their own roots, because the pest that ruined Europe's vineyards cannot live in the ash.

lines.s45.was: Melon de Bourgogne has one job, which is Muscadet, made where the Loire meets the Atlantic near Nantes. The grape itself is quiet: green apple, lemon and a little white peach. The wine is pale, light and bone dry, with brisk acidity and a salty finish. The cellar gives it its character. It rests through the winter on its lees, the spent yeast, which adds a bready note and sometimes a faint prickle. Pour it with oysters, mussels or fried fish. For all its name, it left Burgundy long ago, and it shares both its parents with Chardonnay.

lines.s45.was: Vermentino lives by the sea. Its home is Sardinia, above all the granite hills of Gallura, and it follows the coast through Corsica, Liguria and Tuscany to Provence, where it is called Rolle. It tastes of lime, green apple and white peach, with a scent of wild fennel. It is dry and medium bodied, and it finishes on salt and a touch of bitter almond. Most of it is made cold in steel and sold young, with no oak. Pour it with grilled fish, shellfish or anything with pesto. In Liguria the same grape, with freckled skins, goes by the name Pigato.

lines.sale.was: Vermentino is the seaside white: lime, wild fennel and a salty snap that makes fish taste fresher. I would pour it with the grilled fish or the oysters, as you would squeeze a lemon over them.

lines.s45.was: Godello is the white a Chardonnay drinker should meet next. It comes from Valdeorras, a valley of slate hills inland in Galicia, in north west Spain. It tastes of ripe pear, white peach and lemon, with a stony, faintly salty finish. It is dry and medium to full in body, with fresh acidity. Some is made crisp in steel, and the richer bottles rest on their spent yeast or in barrel for a creamy feel. Pour it with roast fish, scallops or chicken. By the 1970s it had almost died out, until a local project replanted the valley from the few vines left.

lines.s45.was: Savagnin is the white they leave alone in the cask for years. Its home is the Jura, the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland. From a cask kept full it tastes of lemon, green apple and quince, bone dry and sharp. If the cask is never topped up, a veil of yeast grows over the wine, and after six years it is vin jaune. It is golden and still dry, with walnut, curry and a salty tang. Unlike Sherry, it is never strengthened with spirit. Serve it with Comté cheese, morels or chicken in cream. Its squat bottle, the clavelin, holds what is said to be left of a litre.

lines.s45.was: Marsanne does the quiet work in the white wines of the northern Rhône, at Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray. It is not a perfumed grape. It gives ripe pear, white peach and almond, with a waxy feel, a full body and soft acidity. With years in bottle it deepens to honey and toasted hazelnut. The Rhône often ferments it in barrel with a little Roussanne, while Victoria in Australia tends to make it alone, in steel, with no oak at all. Pour it with veal in cream, roast pork or crab. Some of Victoria's vines, planted in 1927, still give a crop each year.

lines.s20.was: Mencía is the red grape of Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra, in Spain's green north west. It is medium bodied and fragrant, with raspberry, violet and a stony note from slate, fresh rather than heavy.

lines.s45.was: Mencía grows on the slate of Spain's green north west, in Bierzo and in the canyons of Ribeira Sacra. In the glass it is bright ruby, with raspberry, sour cherry and violet. It feels fresh and stony, medium in body, with fine tannin. Most cellars handle it gently, in steel or older barrels, so the perfume stays in front, and old vines give deeper, firmer wines that keep. Pour it slightly cool with roast pork, octopus or charcuterie. In Ribeira Sacra the vines hang on stone terraces so steep that the grapes come up in baskets or on little rack railways.

lines.s45.was: Aglianico is southern Italy's mountain red, the grape of Taurasi in the hills of Campania and of Vulture, an extinct volcano in Basilicata. It tastes of black cherry and black plum, with tar, leather and a smoky edge. It is full bodied, with high acidity and firm, drying tannin. Taurasi rests three years before release, at least one in wood, in large old casks or small new barrels that add vanilla. Australia and California grow a little, riper and rounder. Pour it with roast lamb, braised goat or aged hard cheese. In the high vineyards it is picked in November, sometimes after the first snow on the peaks.

lines.s45.was: Blaufränkisch is at home in Burgenland, the eastern edge of Austria along the Hungarian border, and it is the country's red with backbone. It tastes of black cherry and blackberry with a note of cracked black pepper, on bright acidity, firm tannin and a medium to full body. The lighter wines are raised in steel or large old casks and the fuller ones in oak barrels, with less new wood than a generation ago. Pour it with roast duck, venison or a goulash rich with paprika. Hungary calls the same grape Kékfrankos and Germany calls it Lemberger, so you may have met it under another name.

lines.s45.was: Nerello Mascalese climbs Mount Etna on terraces of black lava, past a thousand metres above the Sicilian sea. Many of the vines are old bushes, never grafted. It looks pale, like a Pinot Noir, and tastes of sour cherry, wild strawberry and blood orange, with a smoky, ashy edge. The acidity is high and the tannin fine but firm. Most is aged gently, often in large old casks, so the place speaks louder than the wood. Pour it with grilled tuna, wild mushrooms or roast lamb. DNA has shown that one of its parents is Sangiovese, the grape of Chianti.

lines.s45.was: Touriga Nacional gives Port its backbone, and it leads many of Portugal's dry reds. It was born in the Dão, they say near the village of Tourigo, and made its name in the Douro. lines.s45.was: Carignan was long the workhorse of the Languedoc, and old hillside vines have made its name. It tastes of black raspberry, cranberry and dried cherry, with dried thyme and liquorice. It is deep in colour, with high acidity and firm, rustic tannin. Many cellars ferment the berries whole in a sealed vat, which softens that grip. The Languedoc and Spain tend to be savoury, while old vines in Chile and California are often juicier and more openly fruity. Pour it with cassoulet, grilled sausages or lamb. Spain, where it most likely began, calls it Cariñena or Mazuelo, and old vine growers in Chile share one name for theirs, Vigno.

lines.s45.was: Mourvèdre ripens very late, so it only thrives where the summer is long and hot. Its French home is Bandol, on the Provence coast, and Spain, where it began, calls it Monastrell. lines.s45.was: Sagrantino grows almost nowhere but Montefalco, a hill town in Umbria, the green heart of Italy. lines.s45.was: Carmenère is the grape Bordeaux gave up and Chile kept, grown in the warm valleys of Colchagua and Maipo. It tastes of black plum and blackberry, with roasted red pepper, paprika and a savoury note like soy. It is round and soft, with gentle tannin. lines.s45.was: Roussanne is the fussy grape of the white Rhône, hard to grow and worth the trouble. lines.s45.now: Roussanne tests the patience of growers in the white Rhône, and repays it. It grows from Hermitage down to Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and it climbs into Savoie under the name Bergeron. It smells of ripe pear, honeysuckle and chamomile tea. It is full and silky, with more freshness than its partner, Marsanne. The Rhône tends to blend it and raise it in barrel, while California's Central Coast usually makes it riper and more honeyed. It flatters crab, roast veal or a mushroom risotto. A good many California vines sold as Roussanne in the 1990s turned out to be Viognier.

lines.sale.was: Roussanne is the Rhône white with both richness and lift: honeyed pear and honeysuckle, held up by a fresh finish. I would pour it with the crab or the roast veal, for a table that wants a full white without heavy oak.
lines.sale.now: Roussanne is hard to grow, and one glass shows why growers bother: honeyed pear and honeysuckle, held up by a fresh finish. Try it with the crab or the roast veal.

lines.s45.was: Garganega is the grape in every glass of Soave, at home on hills of dark volcanic rock and pale limestone east of Verona. It tastes of lemon, white peach and ripe pear, and it finishes on a note of bitter almond. It is dry and light to medium in body, fresh without being sharp. Most of it is made in steel tanks and bottled young, with no oak to hide the fruit. Pour it with risotto, lake fish or white asparagus. Dried on racks through the winter, the same grape becomes Recioto di Soave, a golden sweet wine that tastes of honey.

lines.sale.was: Garganega, as a Soave from the hills, is the white for a creamy plate: lemon and white peach to lift it, bitter almond to close it. I would pour it with the risotto, or with the redfish and a squeeze of lemon.

lines.s45.was: Cortese makes Gavi, a crisp white from the south east corner of Piedmont, a region known first for its red wine. It tastes of lemon, green apple and pear, with a stony finish and a faint note of almond. It is light and bone dry, and its acidity is high and bright. The cellar keeps out of the way: steel tanks, no oak and an early bottling, though a little is made sparkling. Serve it cold with oysters, raw fish or a plate of fried seafood. Gavi sits just over the hills from Genoa, and its wine has long gone to the fish restaurants of that coast.

It tastes of ripe apple, pear and a little almond, and it is dry, soft and medium in body. Most of it is made in steel or old casks, and in Alsace it is the main grape of the sparkling wine. Pour it with quiche, river fish or white asparagus. For generations growers planted it mixed with Chardonnay and took the two for one grape.

lines.s10.was: Petit Verdot is the dark seasoning of red Bordeaux, and alone it is inky, with blackberry, violet and a firm grip.
lines.s10.now: Petit Verdot adds colour and grip to red Bordeaux in small doses, and alone it is inky, with blackberry and violet.

lines.s45.was: Petit Verdot means the little green one, because in Bordeaux it ripens so late that some years it never quite does. So the Médoc uses it as seasoning: a few per cent of the blend, for colour, perfume and grip. Tasted alone it is blackberry, black plum and violet, with a pinch of liquorice. It is inky and full, with firm tannin and bright acidity. Warmer places ripen it more surely, and Virginia, Spain and Australia bottle it alone, aged in oak. Pour it with braised short rib, lamb shank or a hard, aged cheese. Even in a blend, a little changes the whole wine.

lines.s45.was: Dolcetto ripens early and drinks early. It is a red of Piedmont, at home around Dogliani and Alba on the cooler slopes that Nebbiolo will not take. Most is kept in steel and bottled young, so the fruit stays in front. Pour it slightly cool with salumi, agnolotti or a mushroom pizza. Little sweet one is what Dolcetto means, though the wine is dry: the name is thought to describe the grapes, low in acid and sweet off the vine.

One village name, Bouzeron, is kept for it alone, and its golden strain has thin skins that turn gold as they ripen.

lines.s45.was: Fiano is a southern white that behaves like a northern one. Its home is Irpinia, the cool, high hills inland from Naples. Most is made in steel and rested on its yeast for texture, and it keeps: in ten years it turns to honey and toast. It has the weight for roast chicken, mushroom pasta or buffalo mozzarella. The Romans are said to have named it for the bees its sweet grapes drew, and the label may still say Apianum.

lines.s45.was: Agiorgitiko takes its name from Saint George, and its home is Nemea, in the north east Peloponnese. It is deep purple, with black plum, black cherry and a touch of cinnamon. The tannin is soft and the feel generous. Altitude shapes it: the warm valley floor gives plush wines, and the cooler hillside villages give firmer, fresher ones. Young Nemea sees little oak, while a Reserve from the slopes takes on vanilla, cedar and tobacco. Pour it with grilled lamb, moussaka or a tomato braise. In Nemea Hercules killed the lion, and the valley's old sweet red was known as the blood of Hercules.

lines.s45.was: Montepulciano grows down the Adriatic side of Italy, and Abruzzo is its heart. It ripens late, into October, and gives a deep purple wine of black cherry and plum. The acidity is soft and the tannin plentiful but round. Most is fermented quickly and bottled young, while a few hill estates age it for years in large casks. Pressed off its skins after a few hours, it also makes Cerasuolo, a cherry red rosé. Pour it with skewers of grilled lamb, sausages or pasta in a meat sauce. Do not confuse it with Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, the Tuscan town's wine, which is Sangiovese.
